{{Resume-like|date=January 2026}}
{{short description|American mathematician}}
'''Benjamin E. Rossman''' is an American mathematician and theoretical computer scientist, specializing in [[computational complexity theory]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Benjamin Rossman, Associate Professor of Computer Science|website=Duke University|url=https://users.cs.duke.edu/~br148/}}</ref> He is currently an associate professor of computer science and mathematics at [[Duke University]].

==Biography==
He graduated from the [[University of Pennsylvania]] with B.A. in 2001 and M.A. in 2002.<ref name=CV>{{cite web|title=Benjamin Rossman, CV|website=University of Toronto|url=http://www.math.toronto.edu/rossman/CV.pdf}}</ref> He received in 2011 his Ph.D. with advisor [[Madhu Sudan]] from [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology|MIT]] with thesis ''Average-Case Complexity of Detecting Cliques''.<ref>{{MathGenealogy|id=155978|title=Benjamin E. Rossman}}</ref><ref>{{cite thesis|author=Rossman, Benjamin|year=2010|title=Average-case complexity of detecting cliques (Doctoral dissertation, Massachusetts Institute of Technology)|publisher=Massachusetts Institute of Technology |hdl=1721.1/62441|type=Thesis }}</ref> From 2010 to 2013 Rossman was a postdoc at the [[Tokyo Institute of Technology]]. From 2013 to 2016 he was an assistant professor in the [[Ken-ichi Kawarabayashi|Kawarabayashi]] Large Graph Project of the [[National Institute of Informatics]]. For the academic year 2014–2015 he was a Simons-Berkeley Research Fellow at the [[Simons Institute for the Theory of Computing]]. He was an assistant professor in the departments of mathematics and computer science of the [[University of Toronto]] until early 2019, before joining [[Duke University]].<ref name=CV/> In the fall of 2018 he was a visiting scientist at the Simons Institute for the Theory of Computing.<ref>{{cite web|title=Benjamin Rossman|website=Simons Institute for the Theory of Computing, U.C. Berkeley campus|date=11 April 2014 |url=https://simons.berkeley.edu/people/benjamin-rossman}}</ref>

{{blockquote|His research seeks to quantify the minimum resources required to solve basic problems in combinatorial models such as [[Boolean circuit]]s. Through creative techniques based in [[mathematical logic|logic]] and the probabilistic method, Ben has derived groundbreaking lower bounds on the [[Computational complexity|complexity]] of detecting [[Clique (graph theory)|clique]]s and determining [[Connectivity (graph theory)|connectivity]] in [[random graph]]s. His other notable results include size and depth [[hierarchy theorem]]s for [[Tree-depth|bounded-depth]] circuits, answering longstanding questions.<ref name=AisenstadtPrize>{{cite web|title=2018 André Aisenstadt Prize in Mathematics Recipient, Ben Rossman (University of Toronto)|website=Centre de Recherches Mathématiques|url=http://www.crm.umontreal.ca/prix/prixAA18_an.shtml|access-date=2019-11-29|archive-date=2019-11-28|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191128215055/http://www.crm.umontreal.ca/prix/prixAA18_an.shtml|url-status=dead}}</ref>}}

Rossman was a [[Sloan Research Fellow]] for the academic year 2017–2018. He won the [[Aisenstadt Prize]] in 2018.<ref name=AisenstadtPrize/> He was an invited speaker at the [[International Congress of Mathematicians]] in 2018 in [[Rio de Janeiro]].<ref>{{cite book|doi=10.1142/9789813272880_0187|chapter=Lower Bounds for Subgraph Isomorphism|title=Proceedings of the International Congress of Mathematicians (ICM 2018)|pages=3425–3446|volume=4|year=2019|last1=Rossman|first1=Benjamin|s2cid=19175568|editor1 =Boyan, Sirakov|editor2=De Souza, Paulo Ney|editor3 = Viana, Marcelo|isbn=978-981-327-287-3|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=iO60DwAAQBAJ&pg=PA3425}}</ref>
